client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't enjoy it. All I keep thinking about is that she's not there, and it kind of ruins everything for me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and being here — it sounds like you're carrying a real heaviness right now, and grief has a way of showing up uninvited, especially in moments that are supposed to feel joyful. The way you described family gatherings, that sense of her absence overshadowing everything, tells me this loss is still very raw and present for you. I'm curious — when you say you're not sure talking will change how you feel, what would "feeling different" even look like for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess "feeling different" would mean... not dreading the holidays so much, or being able to look at her chair at the table without that wave of guilt hitting me all over again. Like maybe I could think about her and it wouldn't feel like I did something wrong just by still being here. But honestly, I don't even know if that's possible — it's been two years and it still feels like yesterday, so part of me wonders if this is just how it's going to be forever now.
therapist: What you just described — that wave of guilt for simply still being here — that's such an important thing to name, and it takes courage to say out loud. It sounds like underneath the grief, there might be a part of you that feels like moving forward somehow betrays her, which is something many people carry but rarely say. I'd gently want to explore that with you — where do you think that sense of guilt first came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think it started the night she died, honestly. I was supposed to visit her that weekend but I canceled because I had work stuff, and then she was just... gone before I got another chance. So in my head, even though I know logically it wasn't my fault, there's this voice that says I chose work over her and now I don't deserve to just go on living my life like nothing happened.
therapist: That moment — canceling the visit, then losing her before you could go back — that's such a painful thing to carry, and it makes complete sense that your mind latched onto it. I notice you said "I know logically it wasn't my fault," and I want to gently stay with that for a moment, because there's often a big gap between what we know in our heads and what we feel in our hearts. What do you think your grandmother would have said if she knew you were punishing yourself like this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I've thought about that a lot, actually. She was the kind of person who would have waved her hand and said something like "don't be silly, you had your reasons." But the thing is, that almost makes it worse, because she was so forgiving and I still feel like I let her down, like I didn't deserve that forgiveness.
therapist: The way you described her — that gentle hand wave, her automatic forgiveness — it's clear how deeply you loved her, and how well you knew her heart. And yet there's something quietly painful in what you're sharing, almost like her kindness feels like it makes the weight heavier rather than lighter, because you don't feel you've *earned* the right to receive it. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you carrying this exact same story, the canceled visit, the guilt, all of it, would you tell them they didn't deserve forgiveness either?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hate that question, because I already know what I'd say to a friend — I'd tell them of course they deserved forgiveness, that one missed visit doesn't erase years of love. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just... doesn't land the same way. It's like there's a different set of rules for me, and I can't figure out how to make them match up.
therapist: You already *know* the compassionate answer — and I can hear how frustrating it is that knowing isn't enough to make it feel true for yourself. That gap you're describing, those "different rules," is actually one of the most common and painful patterns in grief and guilt, and the fact that you can see it so clearly is genuinely meaningful progress, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. I'd love to gently start exploring with you — where do you think you learned that you needed to earn forgiveness, rather than simply receive it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... maybe it came from my dad? Like, growing up, sorry was never really enough — you had to prove you were sorry by doing something, fixing something, making it right in some concrete way. And with my brother's death, there's just nothing I can do to fix it, so I'm stuck in this loop where I keep waiting to earn something that I can never actually earn.
therapist: You just said something really significant — and I noticed that even as the words came out, there was something almost quiet and far-away in how you said them, like part of you was holding something much heavier than what you were letting through. You also mentioned your brother just now, and I want to make sure I heard that right — because that feels like it might be carrying a whole weight of its own that we haven't touched yet. Can you tell me a little more about him?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... my brother. I wasn't even planning to bring him up, it just kind of slipped out, which is maybe why it feels weird to talk about now. We haven't really spoken in almost two years, and most of the time I convince myself it doesn't bother me that much, but sitting here saying it out loud... I don't know, it does bother me, more than I let myself admit.
therapist: The fact that it "just slipped out" tells me some part of you was ready to let it be seen, even if another part wasn't quite prepared for that. And what you just said — "I convince myself it doesn't bother me" — that's such an honest thing to catch yourself doing, and it sounds like sitting here, saying it aloud, is making it harder to keep that convincing going. I'm wondering if the estrangement from your brother and the grief over your grandmother might be tangled together in ways you haven't fully had space to look at yet — does that feel like it might be true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah... I think that might be true, actually. Like, my grandmother was kind of the one who held the family together, and when she died, there was no one left to sort of force me and my brother into the same room anymore. So the estrangement just became... permanent, I guess, and I never really let myself think about how those two losses happened almost at the same time.
therapist: What you just put together in real time — that these two losses are actually one tangled wound — feels like a really important realization, and I imagine it might be sitting with you in a heavy way right now. Losing your grandmother wasn't just losing her; it was also losing the last thread that kept you and your brother connected, and that's an enormous amount of grief to have been carrying without fully naming it. I'm curious — when you imagine what it would mean to truly grieve both of those losses together, what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it's... it's sitting really heavy. Like, I've been telling myself for years that I was okay with how things ended up with my brother, that we just grew apart, that it was nobody's fault. But hearing you say it like that — that losing her took the last thread — I think part of me has been grieving him this whole time and just calling it something else, like stress or just feeling disconnected from people.
therapist: What you just named — that you've been grieving your brother all along, just calling it something else — that's a profound and tender thing to recognize about yourself, and it makes so much sense that it feels heavy right now. "Stress" and "disconnection" were maybe the only containers you had for something that was actually much deeper and much sadder. I want to sit with you in that for a moment — what feels most true to you right now, in this moment, about what you've lost with him?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what I've lost is... the version of him I always thought we'd eventually get back to. Like there was this unspoken assumption that someday we'd just figure it out, have some big conversation, and things would go back to how they were when we were kids. And now I'm realizing that version of him, or maybe that version of us together, might just be gone, and I never even let myself say that out loud before.
therapist: You just said something out loud for the very first time, and I notice there's something almost fragile in the way you're holding it right now — like the words are there, but part of you is still very far away, quietly absorbing what they mean. Grieving a person who is still alive, grieving the *us* you thought you'd someday return to — that's one of the loneliest kinds of loss, because there's no ceremony for it, no one brings you flowers for it. I just want to ask gently — what's happening inside you right now, as you sit with having said that out loud?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
